notes.b: A natural resource is a material or energy source taken from the environment. Sustainable use meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
points: Consumers influence resource use through what they buy, how long they keep products in use and how they dispose of them.
Resources are classed by how quickly they are replaced: renewable resources are replenished naturally, while non-renewable resources are finite.
Consumers conserve resources by buying only what is needed, choosing durable and repairable goods, and using items fully before replacing them.

notes.b: A renewable resource is naturally replenished and is not used up by constant use, provided it is used no faster than it is replaced.
points: Solar energy: photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, and solar thermal panels use sunlight to heat water.
Wind energy: turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity; Irish wind farms are usually sited on exposed upland and coastal land.
Hydroelectric energy: falling water turns turbines, so the source depends on a steady flow of water and a difference in height.
Biomass: wood, straw, energy crops and other plant or animal material are burned, or converted to biogas, to release heat or electricity.
Geothermal energy: heat stored in the earth's crust is brought to the surface as hot water or steam to heat buildings or generate electricity.
Tidal energy uses the rise and fall of the tides to drive turbines; wave energy uses the motion of waves to drive devices.
Renewable sources are sustainable: their supply does not run out on human timescales.
Most produce little or no air pollution or carbon dioxide while generating energy, reducing damage to air and water.
Using renewables reduces dependence on imported fuel, which improves energy security.
Some renewables can be installed in a home, such as solar panels on a roof or a small wind turbine, so energy is produced where it is used.
Building, maintaining and manufacturing renewable systems creates employment.
Limitation: wind and solar output varies with weather and daylight, so storage or a backup supply is needed.

notes.b: A non-renewable resource is limited in supply and cannot be replaced within a human lifetime once it is used up.
points: Fossil fuels are coal, oil, natural gas and peat, formed from the remains of plants and animals over very long periods: peat over thousands of years, coal, oil and gas over millions.
Peat (turf) is dug from bogs for home heating and electricity generation, and bog habitats do not regenerate quickly.
Nuclear energy uses uranium, a mined, finite fuel.
Iron ore, copper ore and bauxite (the ore of aluminium) are non-renewable mineral resources; recycling extends the life of the metal they yield.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas, which contributes to global warming.
Burning coal, oil and peat releases sulphur dioxide, which forms acid rain.
Mining, quarrying and peat extraction destroy habitats and landscapes.
As reserves fall, fuel becomes harder and more costly to extract, so supplies become less secure.
Reduce energy demand, for example by insulating the home and using appliances efficiently, so less fossil fuel is burned.
Choose a renewable electricity supplier, or install a renewable system, where practical.
Buy wood and paper products certified by a recognised scheme such as FSC or PEFC, which confirms that the timber came from managed forests.
Reuse and recycle metals, glass and paper so that finite materials are used again.
Choose products made with recycled content.

keyTerms.definition: A material or energy source taken from the natural environment for human use.
A resource that is naturally replenished and is not used up by constant use, provided it is used no faster than it is replaced.
A resource that is limited in supply and cannot be replaced on human timescales once it is used up.
A resource whose supply is fixed, so it will eventually be used up.
Using resources in a way that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A fuel such as coal, oil, natural gas or peat, formed from the remains of organisms over very long periods.
Plant and animal material used as a fuel, either burned directly or converted to biogas.
Heat stored in the earth's crust, which is used for heating buildings or generating electricity.
A panel that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, that traps heat in the atmosphere.

factCards.definition: Solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, tidal and wave energy.
Coal, oil, natural gas and peat.
They do not run out on human timescales; they produce little or no pollution during operation; they reduce dependence on imported fuel.
Output varies with weather and daylight, so storage or a backup supply is needed; installation costs can be high for systems such as solar panels and turbines.

factCards.term: Three effects of burning fossil fuels
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide adds to global warming; sulphur dioxide forms acid rain; particulates and nitrogen oxides harm the respiratory health of people nearby.

factCards.term: Two ways to conserve energy at home
factCards.definition: Insulate the home to cut heating demand; use appliances efficiently so less electricity is needed.
Iron ore, copper ore and bauxite (aluminium ore).

questions.prompt: Identify two renewable energy sources and describe one environmental benefit of using renewable energy rather than fossil fuels.
questions.model: Two correctly named renewable sources, from solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, tidal and wave energy. One benefit, fully explained: renewable sources produce little or no carbon dioxide or pollution while generating energy, so they reduce global warming and air pollution. Alternatively: they do not run out, so supply is sustainable and does not deplete the environment.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources, giving two examples of each. Describe the environmental effects of using non-renewable energy, and outline how a household can reduce its dependence on it.
questions.model: Definition of a renewable resource as naturally replenished and not used up by constant use, with two named examples such as solar or wind energy. Definition of a non-renewable resource as limited in supply and not replaced once used up, with two named examples such as coal or peat. Environmental effects: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels adds to global warming; sulphur dioxide forms acid rain; mining and peat extraction destroy habitats. Household measures: insulate the home and draught-proof it to reduce heating demand; use appliances efficiently and switch off standby; choose a renewable electricity supplier or install a renewable system such as solar panels; reuse and recycle materials to reduce demand for new resources.
